Question: What is the Official language of Bihar?
Old_Answer: The Official Language of Bihar is Hindi. Bihar was the first Indian state to institutionalize Hindi as state official language in 1881(when it replaced Urdu). The History of Urdu is thus even longer in Bihar. This is the reason Hindi and Urdu are today the first and second official languages of Bihar. The Native spoken Languages are Bhojpuri, Maithili, Magahi, etc but they are not taught in Schools or used in official documents. The associated historical native scripts are also pretty much extinct as Devanagari is the official script. Not only Hindi, but Sanskrit also has good standing in Bihar(usually, that is the 3rd Language in Schools). In our CBSE school located in adjacent Northern Bengal, all Hindi and Sanskrit teachers were either from Bihar or trained there and all had great Pedigree in these Languages. My Younger brother had a Bengali classmate and we were family friends with them. Their mother was also a teacher and had MA/higher studies in Hindi from Bihar. Our Teachers(Singh Sir, Chaudhary Sir, Jha Sir) taught us Shudh Hindi so well that I still haven’t forgotten it.

Question: How similar are Spanish and Portuguese? Are they mutually intelligible?

The people who find more similarities in Languages from same lingusitic family actually have already taken time and interest in learning some words/vocabulary of the other Language. Answer_with_writing_sample: Spanish and Portuguese are indeed quite similar, but they are not mutually intelligible to the same extent that speakers might hope. Both languages are derived from Latin, which gives them a foundation of shared vocabulary and grammar. Having spent time in Southern California, I've encountered numerous instances where Spanish and Portuguese speakers attempted to communicate, sometimes with success, but often relying on gestures or a mix of their languages. For example, I once met a Brazilian who could only speak Portuguese and a Mexican who spoke only Spanish; despite their shared Latin roots, they struggled to understand each other fully. The phonetics can also be a hurdle; for instance, the Portuguese 'ão' sound doesn't exist in Spanish, making pronunciation quite different. Additionally, while there are many cognates—words that look or sound similar across the two languages—there are also false friends that can lead to confusion. For example, 'embarazada' in Spanish means 'pregnant,' while 'embaraçada' in Portuguese means 'embarrassed.' However, speakers of one language can often pick up the other with some exposure, especially if they have a background in romance languages or the desire to learn. In certain contexts, like music or travel, you might find more overlap, but for everyday conversation, proficiency in one does not guarantee understanding of the other. Overall, while the similarities are notable, they are distinct languages that require separate learning to achieve fluency.

Question: Why did the Punjabi language lose its significance in the Punjab province?
Old_Answer: We can make an approximate chronological pattern of ‘Prominent Languages’ of Empires which have ruled over the Punjab region across the Last millennia. Ghaznavid dynasty : 977–1186 , Persian (official and court language; lingua franca) , Arabic (theology), Turkic (military) Ghurid dynasty before 786–1215 , Persian (court, literature) Malmuk Dynasty, 1206–1290, Turkic (main) , Persian (administration) Delhi Sultanate , 1206–1526, Persian (official and court language), Hindavi (semi-official between 1451 and 1526) Mughal Empire, 1526–1857, Persian (official and court language), Urdu (later given official status), Hindustani (lingua franca), Chagatai (spoken in the initial years), Arabic (for religious ceremonies) Sikh Empire , 1799–1849 , Court language (Persian), Spoken languages (Punjabi, Saraiki, Hindko, Pothwari - Pahari, Kangri, Dogri). British Punjab/India, 1849–1947, Urdu (Official Language). West Punjab(Pakistan) has continued with Urdu as it’s official Language. Erstwhile Eastern Punjab(Political) has parts which have Hindi and Punjabi as official Languages. If we analyze this trend, we can see that Punjabi never really had a royal patronage for much of its history. So, Punjabi can’t be compared to Languages like Tamil Or Kannada, or even Urdu/Hindi in that respect. (Dogri/Dogra Akkhar did have Royal Patronage in the hilly regions for a period). But thing is that until 100 or so years ago, this didn’t really harm the language that much. Infact, both Persian and Punjabi thrived in the region for almost 1000 years as mentioned in the following article. The reason for this was that the literacy level was way low during those times, so only the elites would learn Persian or later Urdu. So, Punjabi continued as a famous language of prose and daily use during those times. But over the last 100–150 years, when literacy rates and general mass media consumption started going up, Punjabi or other Languages of the region missed the opportunity to position themselves as a viable languages of governance. This is where the real decline of these Languages started in earnest. (Currently, the erosion is more in Urban regions but over generations it will decline in rural regions too). Still, considering the background of Punjab history, the emergence of Gurmukhi Punjabi can be seen as a success. (half dozen or more ‘Native’ scripts of the region have gone extinct). In this respect, Punjab is different from Bengal, which though also divided over Religion, was still able to maintain and secure its common native Language and Script.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The significance of the Punjabi language in the Punjab province has waned over the years due to various socio-political and cultural factors. During the British colonial period, the imposition of English as the medium of education and administration diminished the status of regional languages, including Punjabi. Post-independence, the language faced challenges in the face of increasing Hindi and Urdu prominence in governance and media, which further marginalized Punjabi. In contemporary times, the rise of globalization has led to a preference for English, especially among the youth, as it is often viewed as a gateway to better career opportunities. Moreover, the emergence of a more homogenized cultural identity has led to the dilution of regional languages. For instance, many Punjabi speakers, especially in urban areas, tend to favor Hindi or English in daily communication, affecting their fluency in Punjabi. Additionally, the political landscape, including the bifurcation of Punjab into Indian and Pakistani regions, has resulted in a disconnect among Punjabi speakers, leading to a fragmented linguistic identity. In education, while Punjabi is taught in some institutions, the lack of resources and qualified teachers hinders its proper instruction, making it less appealing to students. This shift has been further exacerbated by popular media, where Hindi and English dominate, leaving Punjabi underrepresented. Consequently, the combination of these factors has led to a decline in the cultural significance of Punjabi, making it increasingly challenging for the language to maintain its former prominence in its native region.
